identification: The accepted name on the Atlas of Living Australia is Suta flagellum, Little Whip Snake. The Australian Faunal Directory lists Parasuta flagellum among the synonyms (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Suta_flagellum; https://bie.ala.org.au/species/Suta_flagellum). Museums Victoria's species page is still filed as Parasuta flagellum (McCoy, 1878). That page describes a brown body, paler underneath, a black head from the nose to the neck with a pale brown stripe across the top of the nose, and light brown lips, sides of the face and the area below the eyes. It gives a length of up to 40 cm and says the snake is mainly nocturnal (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8792). A direct HTML fetch of that Museums Victoria page failed in this pass. The description is from the indexed text of the same URL. DEECA's 2024 brochure names the Little Whip Snake among common Victorian snakes and does not give a field key (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). It is an elapid. It should not be treated as a harmless snake because it is small. Better Health Channel's Victorian watch-list names tiger snake, copperhead, red-bellied black snake and common or eastern brown snake, and does not name the little whip snake. That list is not a local inventory (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid).
venom: Museums Victoria says the little whip snake is not thought to be highly dangerous to humans, but that any snake bite must be treated with caution (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8792). That is the strongest species-specific danger statement retrieved for this snake. It is not a statement that the bite is harmless, and it is not a measured venom yield. DEECA says the majority of Victoria's snakes are venomous and that young snakes are as venomous as adults (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). The older DELWP sheet says all Victorian elapids are venomous and that even a very young small snake can deliver a lethal bite. That sentence is about the family, not a clinical series for Suta flagellum (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0034/549178/Living-with-snakes-fact-sheet.pdf). Because a glance is a poor way to tell this snake from a juvenile of a larger elapid, the first-aid rule is the same as for any suspected snake bite.
firstAid: Treat every suspected snake bite as an emergency, including a bite from a small snake and a bite where the species is unknown. Better Health Channel says signs are not always visible, a person may not feel the bite, and symptoms may not be obvious for an hour or more. Depending on the snake, symptoms can include pain at the site (immediate or delayed), swelling, bruising or local bleeding, puncture wounds or almost invisible scratches, swollen tender glands in the groin or armpit, faintness, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, headache, abdominal pain, oozing blood from the bite or gums, double or blurred vision, drooping eyelids, trouble speaking or swallowing, limb weakness or paralysis, trouble breathing, and sometimes an initial collapse or confusion followed by partial or complete recovery (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid). Snake-specific first aid on that page is: follow DRSABCD; call triple zero (000) and ask for an ambulance; lie the person down and keep them still; remove jewellery from the limb if you can; apply a broad pressure bandage over the bite and mark the site with an X; apply a further elasticised roller bandage 10–15 cm wide, starting just above the fingers or toes and moving up the limb as far as can be reached, as firmly as possible so a finger cannot easily slide under it; splint the limb; keep the person lying completely still; keep checking colour, temperature and feeling in the fingers or toes; write the time of the bite and of the bandage; mark or photograph the site; do not wash venom off skin or clothes; stay until help arrives; do not walk the person to the vehicle. Do not use a tourniquet, do not cut the bite, do not suck the venom, and do not give alcohol (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid). The same site's general pressure-bandage section, written for several kinds of bites, says the bandage should be firm but not too tight. The snake-specific list is the one to follow for a snake bite, and it matches the Australian and New Zealand Committee on Resuscitation. ANZCOR Guideline 9.4.8, current as of 29 September 2026, recommends the pressure immobilisation technique for all Australian venomous snakes, including sea snakes. If resuscitation is needed it takes precedence (Guideline 8), then apply the bandage as soon as possible. Elasticised bandages 10–15 cm wide are preferred over crepe. The bandage should be firm and tight, so a finger cannot easily slide underneath. A second bandage starts at the fingers or toes and goes up the limb, over clothing if possible, or one bandage can do both jobs by starting at the fingers or toes and including the bite. Splint the joints on both sides of the bite; use a sling for an arm. Keep the person and the limb at rest and bring transport to them. If the person is alone and cannot get help to come, immobilisation is contraindicated after local pressure and they should move to seek urgent help. Do not remove bandages or splints before hospital. A bite that is not on a limb: firm direct pressure, without restricting breathing or chest movement and without firm pressure on the neck or head. Do not cut, suck, wash, or apply an arterial tourniquet. The guideline also says field studies have not shown a clear benefit, and that this may be confounded by poorly applied bandages (https://www.anzcor.org/home/first-aid/guideline-9-4-8-envenomation-pressure-immobilisation-technique; PDF https://www.anzcor.org/assets/generated-anzcor-guideline-pdfs/guideline-9-4-8-envenomation-pressure-immobilisation-technique-296.pdf). A Better Health Channel flood page gives a shorter instruction (clean dry dressing, bite below the heart). That page is not the pressure-immobilisation procedure. It does repeat call 000, do not wash the bite, and do not tourniquet, cut or suck (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/After-a-flood-animal-and-insect-related-hazards). The Victorian Poisons Information Centre, 13 11 26, can advise on bites, but Better Health Channel says not to call it instead of 000 if the person has collapsed, stopped breathing, is fitting, or has anaphylaxis (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/serviceprofiles/victorian-poisons-information-centre-service). Do not catch or kill the snake to identify it. Forest Fire Management Victoria, quoting a DEECA officer, says most bites happen when people try to capture or kill a snake, and that if someone is bitten, call 000 (https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). The older DELWP living-with-snakes sheet says a bite should be treated as serious and that the snake does not need to be identified for antivenom (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0034/549178/Living-with-snakes-fact-sheet.pdf).
activeSeason: Better Health Channel says Australian snakes are most active in the warmer months, spring and summer (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid). DEECA says wild snakes in southern Australia brumate in winter and often come out on sunny days, so a winter encounter is possible (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). The Inverleigh-circle records are not an activity study. Inside 10 km the ALA month facet is May 8, October 5, July 3, August 3, June 2, September 2, December 2, and one each in March, April and November, across 1979–2025 and only 28 rows. Museums Victoria says the species is mainly nocturnal (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8792). Two obscured iNaturalist notes inside the 10 km search, which cannot be mapped, mention animals active together on a 15°C cloudy day (4 May 2024) and an adult with a younger animal (11 August 2024). Those notes are behaviour text, not places.
habitat: Museums Victoria says little whip snakes are found under rocks or logs, especially on stony hills close to grasslands or eucalypt woodlands, in south-eastern mainland Australia (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8792). DEECA's general account, not written for this species alone, says snakes shelter under or in rocks, logs or leaf litter and often within a few hundred metres of water (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). Named records in this circle that describe shelter are survey notes from Bannockburn, in the 5–10 km ring: under tiles in a tile grid at Bannockburn and Bannockburn Bush Reserve, and one eastern brown, not a whip snake, under discarded debris at Bannockburn Bush. Tiles are a survey shelter, not a claim about natural habitat. The Friends of Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve describe about 1,050 ha of grassy woodland between Inverleigh and Teesdale, with Manna Gum and River Red Gum (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). No little whip snake record inside 5 km uses the reserve's name. The 1989 VBA locality is only 'ROUGHLY 4 KM S OF TEESDALE'.
diet: Museums Victoria says little whip snakes hunt mainly small lizards (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8792). No Inverleigh or Bannockburn record opened here names a prey animal. DEECA's general point that snakes eat rodents, and that untidy aviaries attract mice, is not a diet study of this species (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf).
breeding: Museums Victoria says females give birth to about seven live young (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8792). The month of birth, mating season and size at birth are not on that page extract. Papers on litters of Suta flagellum from southern Victoria exist, but they were not read for this file, so they are not used. No local record is described as a birth. An obscured iNaturalist note of one adult and one younger animal is not a litter count and is not a public place.

conservation: A text search of the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act Threatened List, July 2026, found no Suta flagellum, Parasuta flagellum or little whip snake. The only Suta name on that list is Parasuta spectabilis, the Port Lincoln Snake, originally listed as Suta spectabilis, which is a different species (https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0028/793801/FFG_Threatened_List_July_2026.pdf; list page https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/conserving-threatened-species/threatened-list). The EPBC threatened-species extract dated 28 August 2026 has no row for Suta flagellum. The only Notechis row in that file is a different animal, Krefft's Tiger Snake of the Flinders Ranges (https://data.gov.au/data/dataset/ae652011-f39e-4c6c-91b8-1dc2d2dfee8f/resource/78401dce-1f40-49d3-92c4-3713d6e34974/download/20260828spcs.csv). The ALA species page records a New South Wales status of Vulnerable for Suta flagellum and an ACT restricted-trade status. Those are not Victorian FFG categories (https://bie.ala.org.au/species/Suta_flagellum). The same ALA page cites the 2018 IUCN assessment of Parasuta flagellum. The IUCN Red List page itself was not opened, so this file does not restate an IUCN category from the Red List site. Absence from the threatened list does not remove the Wildlife Act protection that applies to all native reptiles (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide).
safety: All native reptiles are protected in Victoria. The Conservation Regulator says it is illegal under the Wildlife Act 1975 to wilfully disturb, hunt, take, trap or kill wildlife without a permit (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). A wildlife-controller licence can cover indigenous reptiles only when they are damaging property or are a danger to people, as set out in the licence conditions. The controller can charge a fee. Relocation of wildlife that is not dangerous still needs an Authority to Control Wildlife even if a licensed controller does the move. Call DEECA on 136 186 (https://www.vic.gov.au/wildlife-controller-licence-guide/wildlife-licences-victoria). An Authority to Control Wildlife is not required if a DEECA-licensed Wildlife Controller is engaged for reptiles that are posing a safety risk to humans (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). DEECA's 2024 Living with Wildlife snakes brochure says never to catch or kill a snake, to keep the yard tidy, to keep pets and children indoors, to clean aviaries so they do not attract mice, to give the snake space and walk away, and to lock dogs and cats away. If a snake is in the house, stay calm, close internal doors, open an external door so it can leave, and call a licensed snake catcher. The brochure says Victoria has more than 25 snake species and that the majority are venomous, and it names the Eastern Brown Snake, Tiger Snake, Red-bellied Black Snake, lowland and highland copperheads, and the Little Whip Snake among common species. It says snakes shelter under or in rocks, logs or leaf litter, often within a few hundred metres of water, and are drawn to houses for water. In southern Australia they brumate in winter but often emerge on sunny days. Most bites occur when people try to catch or kill a snake. Young snakes are as venomous as adults. Out walking: do first-aid training, carry snake bandages, wear closed shoes and loose pants, stay on tracks, and keep dogs on leads (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). Forest Fire Management Victoria's October 2024 snake-season release says the same protection rule in plain words: snakes are protected under the Wildlife Act 1975, and capturing, harming or killing them is illegal. Keep dogs on leads, supervise children and pets, and if a pet is bitten seek a vet immediately. Wildlife crime can be reported to Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. DEECA's contact number is 136 186 (https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). Golden Plains Shire's October 2023 Gazette tells residents the shire has a high population of snakes, that most species seen around homes are venomous, to stay away, to tidy the yard and cut lawns and reduce rats and mice, never to touch, capture or kill a snake, to call 000 if bitten, and to call 136 186 for advice or a trained snake catcher. It repeats that snakes are protected under the Wildlife Act 1975. That notice does not name species and is not a survey of Inverleigh (https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-10/October_2023_Gazette%20_Web_File.pdf). Zoos Victoria's emergency page says, for snakes, contact DEECA on 136 186. For injured wildlife generally it lists Wildlife Victoria on (03) 8400 7300 and Help for Wildlife on 0477 555 611 (https://www.zoo.org.au/emergency-wildlife-help/). For dogs, Animal Welfare Victoria's farm-working-dog guide says a dog bitten by a venomous snake may at first be hyper-excitable, with dilated pupils, muscle twitches, staggering, salivation or vomiting, that the signs change quickly, and that the dog should be taken immediately to a veterinarian. Snake antivenoms are available. The guide is written for farm working dogs and does not give a separate cat procedure (https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/livestock-and-animals/animal-welfare-victoria/dogs/farm-working-dogs/farm-working-dogs-routine-care/Responsible-ownership-of-farm-working-dogs.pdf). No source opened here gives clinical signs that are specific to cats, or a pressure-bandage method for pets. The instruction that is cited is to keep dogs and cats away and, if a pet is bitten, to go to a vet at once (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf; https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). For this species the extra point is size. A snake around 40 cm long can still be an elapid, and Museums Victoria's caution stands beside the rule to call 000 and use pressure immobilisation (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8792; https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid). Families should not pick up a small brown snake to check the head stripe. Pets should be locked away if one is in the yard (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). No little whip snake record in this circle describes a bite to a person, a dog or a cat.

identification: The Australian Museum treats three copperhead species. Lowland copperhead, Austrelaps superbus, is the south-eastern one, including southern Victoria and Tasmania. It gives a total length to 145 cm, with males larger. Shared copperhead features on that page: moderately robust, semi-glossy scales, blackish to grey-brown, sometimes a brownish or orange flush in lowland animals, enlarged paler lowest lateral scales, an obscure neck band or dark vertebral line that is clearer in juveniles, a cream to grey belly, a narrow head barely distinct from the neck, upper labials barred with a whitish front edge, and a round pupil. The coppery snout is not always present (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/copperhead/, updated 16 April 2026). Museums Victoria's lowland copperhead page, also called Common Copperhead, says the body is light grey to red-brown, the underside pale white-yellow to pink-orange, the lips have faint vertical stripes, and the length is up to 1.7 m (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8787). Those two length figures are both published. This file does not collapse 145 cm and 1.7 m into one number. The highland copperhead, Austrelaps ramsayi, and the pygmy copperhead, Austrelaps labialis, are different species on the Australian Museum page. They are not the Inverleigh records, which are identified as Austrelaps superbus.
venom: The Australian Museum says copperhead venom is powerfully neurotoxic, haemolytic and cytotoxic, and that a bite from an adult of any copperhead species may be potentially fatal without medical assistance. It also says copperheads tend to avoid people: if cornered they hiss, flatten and thrash, usually without biting unless provoked further (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/copperhead/). Museums Victoria says the lowland copperhead is dangerously venomous and that the bite can be fatal (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8787). Better Health Channel lists the copperhead among Victorian venomous snakes to watch for, without separating lowland and highland (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid). The pygmy copperhead is the species the Australian Museum discusses as IUCN Vulnerable. That status is not a status for Austrelaps superbus.

activeSeason: Better Health Channel: warmer months, spring and summer, with the caveat from DEECA that southern snakes also emerge on sunny winter days (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid; https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). The Australian Museum cites a southern Victorian study of lowland copperheads: they emerged from winter quiescence in August or September, depending on the year, and entered shelters in late April or early May. habitat: The Australian Museum says the lowland copperhead inhabits grassland, heath, woodland and open scrub, often near marshes, lagoons, swamps, lakes, creeks and rivers, and that it persists in farmland more than a century old, around dams, soaks, drains and road verges. Shelter includes boulders, logs, stumps, roofing iron, dense vegetation, and yabby, rabbit and rodent burrows. Overwintering sites in the account are shallow shelters near water (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/copperhead/). Museums Victoria says damp habitats near streams or swamps (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8787). The local named places are Inverleigh Common and Inverleigh Cemetery. The Friends page describes the Nature Conservation Reserve, between Inverleigh and Teesdale, as grassy woodland of Manna Gum and River Red Gum (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). It says they are cannibalistic (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/copperhead/). The skink-heavy diet is the genus text, not a stomach-content study from Inverleigh. Museums Victoria says females give birth to up to 30 live young in mid to late summer (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8787). Relocation of wildlife that is not dangerous still needs an Authority to Control Wildlife even if a licensed controller does the move. The brochure says Victoria has more than 25 snake species and that the majority are venomous, and it names the Eastern Brown Snake, Tiger Snake, Red-bellied Black Snake, lowland and highland copperheads, and the Little Whip Snake among common species. DEECA's contact number is 136 186 (https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). Golden Plains Shire's October 2023 Gazette tells residents the shire has a high population of snakes, that most species seen around homes are venomous, to stay away, to tidy the yard and cut lawns and reduce rats and mice, never to touch, capture or kill a snake, to call 000 if bitten, and to call 136 186 for advice or a trained snake catcher. That notice does not name species and is not a survey of Inverleigh (https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-10/October_2023_Gazette%20_Web_File.pdf). Zoos Victoria's emergency page says, for snakes, contact DEECA on 136 186. For injured wildlife generally it lists Wildlife Victoria on (03) 8400 7300 and Help for Wildlife on 0477 555 611 (https://www.zoo.org.au/emergency-wildlife-help/). No source opened here gives clinical signs that are specific to cats, or a pressure-bandage method for pets. The cemetery and common records are places people walk. The practical advice from DEECA and the shire is distance, closed shoes, dogs on leads, and a licensed catcher rather than a stick (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf; https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-10/October_2023_Gazette%20_Web_File.pdf). Atlas spelling is 'Inverleigh Cemetary'. The uncertainty is 100 m. It is not a particular grave or path.

Length disagrees: Australian Museum to 145 cm, Museums Victoria up to 1.7 m. Litter size disagrees: average 15 (range 9–45) versus up to 30.

Southern Victorian emergence months are from the study cited by the Australian Museum, not from the three local dates.
Museums Victoria HTML was not fully fetched. The lowland account is the indexed species page.
No local envenoming case was found.

Hatchlings have a dark head and nape patch, and some are banded; the pattern fades. A flesh-pink mouth lining is given as a separation from other Pseudonaja (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). activeSeason: Better Health Channel and DEECA give the general Victorian pattern: spring and summer, plus sunny winter days in the south (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid; https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). The Australian Museum reports a central southern New South Wales transect, not an Inverleigh study: encounters were highest in spring, then autumn, then summer and winter. Snakes were active on mild winter days and basked at an air temperature of 14°C. Males became active earlier. They hunt by day and, when it is hot, in the late afternoon (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). Dated local rows are 19 October 2014, 30 October 2019 and 6 July 1989. The museum specimen from Teesdale has no collection date. Four records do not make a local calendar.
habitat: The Australian Museum says open woodland, scrub and savannah grassland, not rainforest or alpine country, with arid populations along watercourses. It says the species is abundant at agricultural and suburban edges and shelters in logs, rocks, soil cracks, burrows and iron (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). Museums Victoria says most areas, including coastal heath, dry sclerophyll forest and woodland (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8795). The Inverleigh record is in Inverleigh Conservation Reserve, off Common Road. The reserve page describes grassy woodland (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). The Bannockburn Bush record was under discarded debris, which matches the museum's point about disturbed edges, and is one observation.
diet: The Australian Museum says wild eastern brown snakes eat frogs, reptiles and reptile eggs, birds, and mammals, particularly introduced rats and mice. Juveniles take more lizards. They may use venom and constriction, and they can chase prey (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). Museums Victoria says they mostly eat lizards and mammals (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8795). No stomach contents are attached to the Inverleigh or Bannockburn records. DEECA's advice to reduce mice is general snake advice (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf).

The Australian Museum says breeding starts in mid to late spring, males wrestle, yolking follicles run from mid-September to the end of November, and oviducal eggs from late October to late January. Clutch size is up to 25, average 15. Communal nests in rabbit warrens are described. Incubation in that account is 36 days at 30°C and 95 days at 25°C (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). Museums Victoria says females lay up to 35 eggs in cracks in the soil (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8795). The 25 and 35 ceilings are both left standing. No local record is a nest.

The nearest opened observation is 262778568, 23 February 2025, research grade, accuracy 23 m, place guess Bannockburn VIC 3331, about 13.4 km, description 'Juvenile snake a dog killed.' That is outside the 10 km tier. It is evidence of a dog killing a snake at Bannockburn, not an Inverleigh hangout (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/262778568).
conservation: The Australian Museum says the species is not endangered in its account, because it uses disturbed country and eats house mice (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). It is not in the July 2026 FFG Threatened List text search for Pseudonaja or brown snake. Other snakes are listed, including the inland taipan under the name Small-scaled Snake, Oxyuranus microlepidotus, which is not this species and is not in the Inverleigh radii (https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0028/793801/FFG_Threatened_List_July_2026.pdf). It is not in the 28 August 2026 EPBC extract (https://data.gov.au/data/dataset/ae652011-f39e-4c6c-91b8-1dc2d2dfee8f/resource/78401dce-1f40-49d3-92c4-3713d6e34974/download/20260828spcs.csv). It is still protected wildlife. Killing one on a farm is not legal (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide; https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). The Australian Museum notes predators including birds of prey and feral cats, and that many are killed on roads and by landowners (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). Those predator statements are not local carcass records, apart from the dog-killed juvenile outside the 10 km circle.
safety: All native reptiles are protected in Victoria. The Conservation Regulator says it is illegal under the Wildlife Act 1975 to wilfully disturb, hunt, take, trap or kill wildlife without a permit (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). A wildlife-controller licence can cover indigenous reptiles only when they are damaging property or are a danger to people, as set out in the licence conditions. The controller can charge a fee. Relocation of wildlife that is not dangerous still needs an Authority to Control Wildlife even if a licensed controller does the move. Call DEECA on 136 186 (https://www.vic.gov.au/wildlife-controller-licence-guide/wildlife-licences-victoria). An Authority to Control Wildlife is not required if a DEECA-licensed Wildlife Controller is engaged for reptiles that are posing a safety risk to humans (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). DEECA's 2024 Living with Wildlife snakes brochure says never to catch or kill a snake, to keep the yard tidy, to keep pets and children indoors, to clean aviaries so they do not attract mice, to give the snake space and walk away, and to lock dogs and cats away. If a snake is in the house, stay calm, close internal doors, open an external door so it can leave, and call a licensed snake catcher. The brochure says Victoria has more than 25 snake species and that the majority are venomous, and it names the Eastern Brown Snake, Tiger Snake, Red-bellied Black Snake, lowland and highland copperheads, and the Little Whip Snake among common species. It says snakes shelter under or in rocks, logs or leaf litter, often within a few hundred metres of water, and are drawn to houses for water. In southern Australia they brumate in winter but often emerge on sunny days. Most bites occur when people try to catch or kill a snake. Young snakes are as venomous as adults. Out walking: do first-aid training, carry snake bandages, wear closed shoes and loose pants, stay on tracks, and keep dogs on leads (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). Forest Fire Management Victoria's October 2024 snake-season release says the same protection rule in plain words: snakes are protected under the Wildlife Act 1975, and capturing, harming or killing them is illegal. Keep dogs on leads, supervise children and pets, and if a pet is bitten seek a vet immediately. Wildlife crime can be reported to Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. DEECA's contact number is 136 186 (https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). Golden Plains Shire's October 2023 Gazette tells residents the shire has a high population of snakes, that most species seen around homes are venomous, to stay away, to tidy the yard and cut lawns and reduce rats and mice, never to touch, capture or kill a snake, to call 000 if bitten, and to call 136 186 for advice or a trained snake catcher. It repeats that snakes are protected under the Wildlife Act 1975. That notice does not name species and is not a survey of Inverleigh (https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-10/October_2023_Gazette%20_Web_File.pdf). Zoos Victoria's emergency page says, for snakes, contact DEECA on 136 186. For injured wildlife generally it lists Wildlife Victoria on (03) 8400 7300 and Help for Wildlife on 0477 555 611 (https://www.zoo.org.au/emergency-wildlife-help/). For dogs, Animal Welfare Victoria's farm-working-dog guide says a dog bitten by a venomous snake may at first be hyper-excitable, with dilated pupils, muscle twitches, staggering, salivation or vomiting, that the signs change quickly, and that the dog should be taken immediately to a veterinarian. Snake antivenoms are available. The guide is written for farm working dogs and does not give a separate cat procedure (https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/livestock-and-animals/animal-welfare-victoria/dogs/farm-working-dogs/farm-working-dogs-routine-care/Responsible-ownership-of-farm-working-dogs.pdf). No source opened here gives clinical signs that are specific to cats, or a pressure-bandage method for pets. The instruction that is cited is to keep dogs and cats away and, if a pet is bitten, to go to a vet at once (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf; https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). This is the species the Australian Museum associates with the largest number of Australian snakebite deaths, and the local animal crossed a reserve track in front of a car. The response on a track is to stop and let it leave, not to get out and move it (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/; occurrence a1426a55). Dogs are part of the local picture only outside the tier: the February 2025 Bannockburn observation is a juvenile a dog killed, about 13.4 km away. Inside 10 km there is no pet-bite record. Keep dogs on leads and lock them away if a snake is in the yard (https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe; https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). The painless-bite warning means a person who thinks they were only scratched should still call 000 and start pressure immobilisation (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/; https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid).
notWellDocumented: One record inside 5 km, and four ALA rows inside 10 km. No iNaturalist record inside 10 km. Absence of more records is not proof the species is rare on farms.

identification: Inside 5 km and inside 10 km of -38.10, 144.05, the only snakes in the Atlas of Living Australia Elapidae species facet are the little whip snake (Suta flagellum), the lowland copperhead (Austrelaps superbus) and the eastern brown snake (Pseudonaja textilis). Class Reptilia at those radii also has skinks and dragons, and at 10 km four freshwater-turtle records (Chelidae). Explicit searches for pythons, blind snakes, colubrids, boas and filesnakes returned 0 records at 5, 10, 20 and 50 km. DEECA says Victoria has only two python species, the diamond python and the carpet python (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). Neither appears in this circle. At 20 km, ALA Elapidae adds the tiger snake (Notechis scutatus, 3) and one white-lipped snake (Drysdalia coronoides). The red-bellied black snake (Pseudechis porphyriacus) is still 0 at 20 km. At 50 km the ALA Elapidae facet is little whip snake 437, lowland copperhead 370, tiger snake 361, eastern brown snake 203, white-lipped snake 47, red-bellied black snake 23, small-eyed snake Cryptophis nigrescens 5, yellow-bellied sea snake Hydrophis platurus 5, and one Port Lincoln snake Suta spectabilis. The sea snake records are not Inverleigh animals. iNaturalist species counts for Serpentes (taxon 85553), all grades, match the task: 5 km little whip snake 7 and lowland copperhead 1; 10 km little whip snake 16 and lowland copperhead 1. Research grade is the same at 5 km, and at 10 km the little whip snake drops from 16 to 15 because one observation is needs identification. People often expect tiger snakes and red-bellied black snakes. Better Health Channel lists both, with the copperhead and the common or eastern brown snake, as Victorian venomous snakes to watch for, and says the tiger snake is the most common cause of snake envenoming in Victoria (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid). DEECA's brochure names the same set, plus the little whip snake, as common Victorian species (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). Golden Plains Shire says the shire has a high population of snakes and that most species around houses are venomous, without naming them (https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-10/October_2023_Gazette%20_Web_File.pdf). Those are statewide or shire statements. They are not records inside 10 km of Inverleigh. On the data pulled here, tiger snakes and red-bellied black snakes are not recorded within 5 km or 10 km. The nearest tiger snake record is a November 2024 museum specimen at Saffin Court, Bannockburn, about 11.8 km away. The nearest red-bellied black snake is a December 1989 atlas record about 28.4 km away, roughly 2 km west of Fairy Park. Lack of a record is not proof a snake never crosses the radius.
venom: Danger is not the same for every species, and first aid is. Eastern brown snake: Australian Museum, more deaths than any other Australian snake, neurotoxic and procoagulant venom, bite often painless, can be fatal (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). Lowland copperhead: Australian Museum, powerfully neurotoxic, haemolytic and cytotoxic, a bite from an adult potentially fatal without medical help; Museums Victoria, dangerously venomous and the bite can be fatal (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/copperhead/; https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8787). Little whip snake: Museums Victoria, not thought highly dangerous, but any bite treated with caution. It is still an elapid (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8792). Tiger snake, not recorded inside 10 km: Australian Museum, venom strongly neurotoxic and coagulant, extremely dangerous (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/tiger-snake/, updated 16 July 2026). Museums Victoria says the venom is toxic to humans and the bite potentially lethal (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8791). Red-bellied black snake, not recorded inside 20 km: Australian Museum, anticoagulant and myotoxic venom, probably the least dangerous Australian elapid for its size, few confirmed deaths, many bites mild, but hospitalisations occur and children and pets are at greater risk because they are smaller. Treat every suspected bite as serious (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/red-bellied-black-snake/, updated 16 July 2026). Museums Victoria says potentially lethal (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8794). DEECA says young snakes are as venomous as adults, and that a non-venomous snake can still bite painfully. No non-venomous snake family was recorded within 50 km (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf).
firstAid: Treat every suspected snake bite as an emergency, including a bite from a small snake and a bite where the species is unknown. Better Health Channel says signs are not always visible, a person may not feel the bite, and symptoms may not be obvious for an hour or more. Depending on the snake, symptoms can include pain at the site (immediate or delayed), swelling, bruising or local bleeding, puncture wounds or almost invisible scratches, swollen tender glands in the groin or armpit, faintness, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, headache, abdominal pain, oozing blood from the bite or gums, double or blurred vision, drooping eyelids, trouble speaking or swallowing, limb weakness or paralysis, trouble breathing, and sometimes an initial collapse or confusion followed by partial or complete recovery (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid). Snake-specific first aid on that page is: follow DRSABCD; call triple zero (000) and ask for an ambulance; lie the person down and keep them still; remove jewellery from the limb if you can; apply a broad pressure bandage over the bite and mark the site with an X; apply a further elasticised roller bandage 10–15 cm wide, starting just above the fingers or toes and moving up the limb as far as can be reached, as firmly as possible so a finger cannot easily slide under it; splint the limb; keep the person lying completely still; keep checking colour, temperature and feeling in the fingers or toes; write the time of the bite and of the bandage; mark or photograph the site; do not wash venom off skin or clothes; stay until help arrives; do not walk the person to the vehicle. Do not use a tourniquet, do not cut the bite, do not suck the venom, and do not give alcohol (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid). The same site's general pressure-bandage section, written for several kinds of bites, says the bandage should be firm but not too tight. The snake-specific list is the one to follow for a snake bite, and it matches the Australian and New Zealand Committee on Resuscitation. ANZCOR Guideline 9.4.8, current as of 29 September 2026, recommends the pressure immobilisation technique for all Australian venomous snakes, including sea snakes. If resuscitation is needed it takes precedence (Guideline 8), then apply the bandage as soon as possible. Elasticised bandages 10–15 cm wide are preferred over crepe. The bandage should be firm and tight, so a finger cannot easily slide underneath. A second bandage starts at the fingers or toes and goes up the limb, over clothing if possible, or one bandage can do both jobs by starting at the fingers or toes and including the bite. Splint the joints on both sides of the bite; use a sling for an arm. Keep the person and the limb at rest and bring transport to them. If the person is alone and cannot get help to come, immobilisation is contraindicated after local pressure and they should move to seek urgent help. Do not remove bandages or splints before hospital. A bite that is not on a limb: firm direct pressure, without restricting breathing or chest movement and without firm pressure on the neck or head. Do not cut, suck, wash, or apply an arterial tourniquet. The guideline also says field studies have not shown a clear benefit, and that this may be confounded by poorly applied bandages (https://www.anzcor.org/home/first-aid/guideline-9-4-8-envenomation-pressure-immobilisation-technique; PDF https://www.anzcor.org/assets/generated-anzcor-guideline-pdfs/guideline-9-4-8-envenomation-pressure-immobilisation-technique-296.pdf). A Better Health Channel flood page gives a shorter instruction (clean dry dressing, bite below the heart). That page is not the pressure-immobilisation procedure. It does repeat call 000, do not wash the bite, and do not tourniquet, cut or suck (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/After-a-flood-animal-and-insect-related-hazards). The Victorian Poisons Information Centre, 13 11 26, can advise on bites, but Better Health Channel says not to call it instead of 000 if the person has collapsed, stopped breathing, is fitting, or has anaphylaxis (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/serviceprofiles/victorian-poisons-information-centre-service). Do not catch or kill the snake to identify it. Forest Fire Management Victoria, quoting a DEECA officer, says most bites happen when people try to capture or kill a snake, and that if someone is bitten, call 000 (https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). The older DELWP living-with-snakes sheet says a bite should be treated as serious and that the snake does not need to be identified for antivenom (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0034/549178/Living-with-snakes-fact-sheet.pdf).
activeSeason: Better Health Channel: most active in spring and summer (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid). DEECA: in southern Australia they brumate in winter and often emerge on sunny days, so winter is not a zero-risk season (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). Golden Plains Shire's October 2023 notice expects sightings to increase as the weather warms (https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-10/October_2023_Gazette%20_Web_File.pdf). Species accounts add detail that should not be flattened: lowland copperheads in a southern Victorian study emerged about August or September and retreated in late April or early May (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/copperhead/); eastern brown snakes in a southern New South Wales study were most often seen in spring and were active on mild winter days (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). Local month facets are record dates. They are listed on each species object. They are not a phenology study.
habitat: DEECA: rocks, logs, leaf litter, often within a few hundred metres of water, and yards that offer water or mice (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). The shire notice: long grass, rubbish and rodents bring snakes closer to houses (https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-10/October_2023_Gazette%20_Web_File.pdf). Named places that actually appear on non-obscured records inside 10 km are Inverleigh Common, Inverleigh Cemetery, Inverleigh Conservation Reserve off Common Road, a public iNaturalist point whose place guess is only Inverleigh, a VBA point 'roughly 4 km south of Teesdale', Bannockburn Bush and Bannockburn Bush Reserve, Harvey Road paddocks at Bannockburn, rough distances south-west of Lownde Bridge, a coarse 'Geelong area, Teesdale' museum point, and a coarse '10 km NNE of Winchelsea' museum point. No record string inside 10 km names the Leigh River bank, the Hamilton Highway, or a particular home. Those places are not invented here. Corangamite CMA was searched for a snake page in the earlier pass and none was found that lists species at Inverleigh. A Wadawurrung word list in a flows study names a snake as food. That is cultural text, not an occurrence, and it is not used as a species record.
diet: Diets differ and are on the species objects: little whip snake mainly small lizards (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8792); lowland copperhead frogs, lizards and small mammals on the Museums Victoria page, and a skink-heavy genus account on the Australian Museum page (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8787; https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/copperhead/); eastern brown snake frogs, reptiles, birds and especially rats and mice (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). Tiger snakes, outside this radius, take fish, frogs, tadpoles, lizards, birds, mammals and carrion (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/tiger-snake/). Red-bellied black snakes, also outside, take frogs, reptiles, small mammals and other snakes (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/red-bellied-black-snake/; https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8794). The household consequence DEECA and the shire both draw is that mice and rats are a reason a snake comes to a yard (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf; https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-10/October_2023_Gazette%20_Web_File.pdf).
breeding: Do not mix the modes. Little whip snake, lowland copperhead, tiger snake and red-bellied black snake bear live young in the museum accounts. The eastern brown snake lays eggs (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8792; https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8787; https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8791; https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8794; https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/eastern-brown-snake/). Litter and clutch numbers disagree between the Australian Museum and Museums Victoria for the copperhead and the brown snake. They are quoted on the species objects and not averaged. No birth or nest is in the Inverleigh records.
hangouts: Use the species objects for places inside 5 km and in the 5–10 km ring. This object only records the nearest evidence for the snakes that are not in those tiers, so they are not dropped into Inverleigh by expectation. Tiger snake: zero ALA and zero iNaturalist inside 10 km. Nearest ALA is Museums Victoria, Bannockburn, Saffin Court, 17 November 2024, about 11.8 km. Nearest open iNaturalist point is Donaldson Road, Lethbridge, 11 October 2026, about 16.6 km. Other tiger snake points inside 25 km on iNaturalist are around 22–25 km (Fyansford, Highton, Newtown, Lovely Banks, Gherang), including roadkill. One research-grade observation, 203092052, says the snake was killed by a domestic animal; it is location-obscured, about 22 km on the public coordinate, and is not a place. Red-bellied black snake: zero inside 20 km on ALA and on iNaturalist. Nearest ALA is about 28.4 km, 'roughly 2 km west of Fairy Park', December 1989. Research-grade iNaturalist clusters around Staughton Vale and Brisbane Ranges National Park, about 31 km and beyond. White-lipped snake: one ALA record at about 18.3 km on the Mount Mercer–Shelford road at Shelford, April 2018, and zero iNaturalist inside 25 km. It is not given a species object because it is outside 10 km. iNaturalist at 50 km, all grades, also returned one boomslang (Dispholidus typus) and one Children's python (Antaresia childreni). Both disappear from the research-grade counts. They are not treated as wild Inverleigh snakes. Obscured little whip snake coordinates inside 5 km and 10 km are counted and are not mapped.
conservation: Protection and threatened status are different. Every native reptile is protected under the Wildlife Act 1975 whether or not it is on a threatened list (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide; https://www.vic.gov.au/wildlife-controller-licence-guide/wildlife-licences-victoria; https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). July 2026 FFG Threatened List: text search found no Austrelaps, no Pseudonaja, no Notechis, no Pseudechis porphyriacus, no Suta flagellum and no Drysdalia coronoides. Snake taxa that are on that list include the bandy bandy (Vermicella annulata), bardick (Echiopsis curta), common death adder (Acanthophis antarcticus), carpet python (Morelia spilota metcalfei), diamond python (Morelia spilota spilota), De Vis' banded snake (Denisonia devisi), Masters' snake (Drysdalia mastersii), Port Lincoln snake (Parasuta spectabilis), red-naped snake (Furina diadema) and small-scaled snake (Oxyuranus microlepidotus). None of those is in the 10 km Inverleigh snake facet (https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0028/793801/FFG_Threatened_List_July_2026.pdf). EPBC extract of 28 August 2026: the only hit among these names is Notechis scutatus ater, Krefft's Tiger Snake (Flinders Ranges), Vulnerable, SPRAT taxon 82287. That is not the Victorian tiger snake. Austrelaps superbus, Pseudonaja textilis, Suta flagellum, Pseudechis porphyriacus and mainland Notechis scutatus are not rows in that extract (https://data.gov.au/data/dataset/ae652011-f39e-4c6c-91b8-1dc2d2dfee8f/resource/78401dce-1f40-49d3-92c4-3713d6e34974/download/20260828spcs.csv; http://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/sprat/public/publicspecies.pl?taxon_id=82287). safety: All native reptiles are protected in Victoria. The Conservation Regulator says it is illegal under the Wildlife Act 1975 to wilfully disturb, hunt, take, trap or kill wildlife without a permit (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). A wildlife-controller licence can cover indigenous reptiles only when they are damaging property or are a danger to people, as set out in the licence conditions. The controller can charge a fee. Relocation of wildlife that is not dangerous still needs an Authority to Control Wildlife even if a licensed controller does the move. Call DEECA on 136 186 (https://www.vic.gov.au/wildlife-controller-licence-guide/wildlife-licences-victoria). An Authority to Control Wildlife is not required if a DEECA-licensed Wildlife Controller is engaged for reptiles that are posing a safety risk to humans (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide). DEECA's 2024 Living with Wildlife snakes brochure says never to catch or kill a snake, to keep the yard tidy, to keep pets and children indoors, to clean aviaries so they do not attract mice, to give the snake space and walk away, and to lock dogs and cats away. If a snake is in the house, stay calm, close internal doors, open an external door so it can leave, and call a licensed snake catcher. The brochure says Victoria has more than 25 snake species and that the majority are venomous, and it names the Eastern Brown Snake, Tiger Snake, Red-bellied Black Snake, lowland and highland copperheads, and the Little Whip Snake among common species. It says snakes shelter under or in rocks, logs or leaf litter, often within a few hundred metres of water, and are drawn to houses for water. In southern Australia they brumate in winter but often emerge on sunny days. Most bites occur when people try to catch or kill a snake. Young snakes are as venomous as adults. Out walking: do first-aid training, carry snake bandages, wear closed shoes and loose pants, stay on tracks, and keep dogs on leads (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf). Forest Fire Management Victoria's October 2024 snake-season release says the same protection rule in plain words: snakes are protected under the Wildlife Act 1975, and capturing, harming or killing them is illegal. Keep dogs on leads, supervise children and pets, and if a pet is bitten seek a vet immediately. Wildlife crime can be reported to Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. DEECA's contact number is 136 186 (https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). Golden Plains Shire's October 2023 Gazette tells residents the shire has a high population of snakes, that most species seen around homes are venomous, to stay away, to tidy the yard and cut lawns and reduce rats and mice, never to touch, capture or kill a snake, to call 000 if bitten, and to call 136 186 for advice or a trained snake catcher. It repeats that snakes are protected under the Wildlife Act 1975. That notice does not name species and is not a survey of Inverleigh (https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-10/October_2023_Gazette%20_Web_File.pdf). Zoos Victoria's emergency page says, for snakes, contact DEECA on 136 186. For injured wildlife generally it lists Wildlife Victoria on (03) 8400 7300 and Help for Wildlife on 0477 555 611 (https://www.zoo.org.au/emergency-wildlife-help/). For dogs, Animal Welfare Victoria's farm-working-dog guide says a dog bitten by a venomous snake may at first be hyper-excitable, with dilated pupils, muscle twitches, staggering, salivation or vomiting, that the signs change quickly, and that the dog should be taken immediately to a veterinarian. Snake antivenoms are available. The guide is written for farm working dogs and does not give a separate cat procedure (https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/livestock-and-animals/animal-welfare-victoria/dogs/farm-working-dogs/farm-working-dogs-routine-care/Responsible-ownership-of-farm-working-dogs.pdf). No source opened here gives clinical signs that are specific to cats, or a pressure-bandage method for pets. The instruction that is cited is to keep dogs and cats away and, if a pet is bitten, to go to a vet at once (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf; https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe). Call order for a bite: 000 first, pressure immobilisation, stay still. The poisons line 13 11 26 is not the emergency number if the person has collapsed (https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/healthyliving/bites-and-stings-first-aid; https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/serviceprofiles/victorian-poisons-information-centre-service; https://www.anzcor.org/home/first-aid/guideline-9-4-8-envenomation-pressure-immobilisation-technique). Call order for a snake in the yard or the house, when nobody has been bitten: do not catch or kill it; lock dogs and cats away; keep people clear; call a DEECA-licensed wildlife controller. DEECA on 136 186 can provide a list. The list is not an endorsement, and the department does not itself come and remove the snake. The controller is user-pays (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf; https://www.vic.gov.au/wildlife-controller-licence-guide/wildlife-licences-victoria; https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0034/549178/Living-with-snakes-fact-sheet.pdf; https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2023-10/October_2023_Gazette%20_Web_File.pdf). You do not need an Authority to Control Wildlife when the controller is engaged because the reptile is a safety risk. You do need one if the animal is being moved for another reason (https://www.vic.gov.au/authority-control-wildlife-application-guide; https://www.vic.gov.au/wildlife-controller-licence-guide/wildlife-licences-victoria). For a dog or a cat: keep them away before a bite happens. If a pet is bitten, Animal Welfare Victoria's signs for dogs are a starting picture, and the cited action is an immediate vet visit, where antivenom can be used. Do not wait out the signs. Cat-specific signs were not in the sources opened (https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/livestock-and-animals/animal-welfare-victoria/dogs/farm-working-dogs/farm-working-dogs-routine-care/Responsible-ownership-of-farm-working-dogs.pdf; https://www.ffm.vic.gov.au/media-releases/snake-season-is-here,-be-prepared-and-stay-safe; https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/714580/Living-with-Wildlife-Snakes.pdf).
